blocks.text: Almost every backtracking question fits one of two templates, and the difference is the **shape of the decision tree** — what you choose at each level. Add **pruning** — refusing to explore a branch that can't work — and the same template solves puzzles that would otherwise take forever.

Walk the items in order. At each item there are exactly two choices: **take it** or **skip it**. The tree is binary and n levels deep, with 2ⁿ leaves — one per subset. Subsets, Target Sum and many "pick some items" problems look like this.

blocks.code:
solve(i):
    if i == n:  record the path; return
    path.add(items[i]);  solve(i + 1);  path.remove()     # take items[i]
    solve(i + 1)                                          # skip items[i]

blocks.text: At each level, loop over **every option still allowed** and try each in turn. The tree can have many branches per node. Two common rules decide what's allowed:

items: **Combinations** (order doesn't matter): pass a `start` index and only choose items at or after it, so `{1, 2}` is never built again as `{2, 1}`.
**Permutations** (order matters): any item not used yet — track them in a `used` array.

blocks.code:
solve(start):
    if the path is complete:  record a copy; return
    for each choice c allowed from start:
        if c breaks a rule: continue          # prune
        path.add(c);  solve(next);  path.remove()

blocks.text: Most backtracking problems have **rules**. Checking a rule only at the leaves wastes the whole subtree; checking it **as soon as a choice is made** cuts the branch off before any of its descendants are built. The example: binary strings of length n with **no two 1s next to each other**. A 1 right after a 1 can never be fixed later, so don't explore it at all.

blocks.alt: Binary strings of length 3 with no two adjacent 1s. The search never builds 11 or 011: as soon as a 1 would follow a 1, that branch is cut. The five leaves are 000, 001, 010, 100 and 101.

elements.text: no two 1s next to each other: a branch dies the moment it breaks the rule
elements.originalText: no two 1s next to each other: a branch dies the moment it breaks the rule

blocks.caption: Each branch that would put a 1 after a 1 is cut before it's explored.

blocks.code:
def no_adjacent_ones(n):
    result, path = [], []

    def build():
        if len(path) == n:
            result.append("".join(path))
            return
        path.append("0")                  # a 0 is always allowed
        build()
        path.pop()
        if not path or path[-1] != "1":   # prune: a 1 right after a 1 can never work
            path.append("1")
            build()
            path.pop()

    build()
    return result

blocks.text: The answers grow like the Fibonacci numbers (about 1.6ⁿ) instead of 2ⁿ, and the search does work only for strings that can still succeed. On harder puzzles — N-Queens, Sudoku — pruning is the difference between milliseconds and years.

blocks.code:
problem                      leaves (answers)        time
subsets of n                 2^n                     O(2^n · n)
combinations, k of n         C(n, k)                 O(C(n, k) · k)
permutations of n            n!                      O(n! · n)
k choices at each of n steps k^n                     O(k^n · n)

space: O(n) for the path and the call stack, plus the output

blocks.text: The extra factor n is for copying each answer. Pruning can't change these worst cases, but in practice it often cuts the tree down enormously.

items: **Recording the path itself** instead of a copy — later un-choose steps then empty every stored answer.
**Forgetting to un-choose** — the next branch starts with leftovers from the last one.
**Duplicates** — when the input has repeated values, sort it and skip a value equal to the one just tried at the same level (Subsets II, Permutations II).
**Pruning too late** — checking a rule only at the leaves explores the whole dead subtree.
**Include / exclude** builds a binary tree of subsets; **loop over choices** builds combinations (with `start`) or permutations (with `used`).
**Prune** the moment a partial path breaks a rule.
Time ≈ number of nodes in the decision tree × work per node; space = the depth.
Sort and skip equal neighbours to avoid duplicate answers.
